summary: Federal AI use is publicly inventoried; GAO audits it, and the state legislatures writing AI law are tracked on this site.

analysis.body:
The U.S. Government Accountability Office documented that twenty of twenty-three major federal agencies reported approximately 1,200 current and planned AI use cases, covering specific challenges or opportunities that AI may address, while three agencies reported having no uses for AI at all. Of those roughly 1,200 cases, only about 200 represented AI systems that agencies were actually using in production at the time of GAO's review, meaning most reported use cases remained in planning phases rather than active deployment. Reported operational applications included analyzing data from cameras and radar to identify border activities, reviewing photographs from drones, and targeting scientific specimens for planetary rovers, with NASA and the Department of Commerce reporting the highest numbers of use cases among the agencies surveyed.

GAO also found serious data quality problems in the inventories agencies submitted. Five agencies provided comprehensive information for each of their reported use cases, but the other fifteen had instances of incomplete and inaccurate data, including missing required fields such as the AI life cycle stage, and two agencies submitted inventories that included items later determined not to be AI at all. GAO concluded that without accurate inventories, the government's management of AI will be hindered by incomplete and inaccurate data.

On the compliance side, ten of twenty-three agencies implemented all AI requirements specific to their agencies, twelve implemented some but not all, and one was exempt. The Office of Management and Budget had not yet developed government-wide guidance on how agencies should acquire and use AI, a gap GAO identified as preventing agencies from consistently managing AI. The Office of Personnel Management had not established or updated an occupational category for employees performing AI work, and the Office of Science and Technology Policy had not communicated which agencies were expected to fulfill specific requirements. Commerce and the General Services Administration were among the few that fully implemented their selected requirements, with Commerce creating a plan for AI technical standards and GSA establishing an AI Center of Excellence.

The President's fiscal year 2023 budget request included 1.8 billion dollars for nondefense research and development investment in AI, providing a rough measure of federal financial commitment to the technology. Beyond spending, the policy and legal environment surrounding government AI use is dense and evolving rapidly. The law tracker on theworldofai.org monitors 2,440 AI bills across 53 jurisdictions, updated daily, representing the breadth of legislative activity at the state level. OECD.AI tracks national AI strategies, public-sector initiatives, and ethical frameworks across member and partner countries, and Oxford Insights publishes a Government AI Readiness Index that scores countries on policy capacity, governance, infrastructure, and public-sector adoption, providing a standard cross-national comparison for policymakers assessing where their country stands relative to peers.

Stanford HAI's annual AI Index, described as one of the most credible and authoritative sources for data and insights on artificial intelligence, carries a government and policy track covering legislation counts, national strategy execution, and public-sector procurement, and it has been referenced by high-level policymakers in the United States, the United Kingdom, and the European Union. Stanford HAI has also noted a widening gap between what AI can do and how prepared governments are to manage it, observing that the frameworks needed to govern, evaluate, and understand the technology are falling behind its rapid integration. For any organization or government body considering AI deployment, the GAO record suggests that documenting use cases accurately, meeting existing compliance requirements, and ensuring acquisition guidance is in place before expanding deployment are the practical first steps, rather than assuming that policy frameworks will keep pace with procurement.
